A beginner first practises the open and muted sounds of the heads and the shell pattern (cáscara), keeping the beat with a cowbell or a cymbal; then comes the baqueteo, the mambo, the chachachá and similar strokes. More advanced players work on the rolls and rim shots used in solos, and on striking the head and the bongo bell at the same time.

蒂姆巴雷斯鼓是美洲古巴的膜鳴樂器，由淺身單面鼓組成，鼓殼多為金屬、底部開口，鼓面: The timbales are a membranophone of Cuba in the Americas, made up of shallow single-headed drums, the shell usually of metal and open at the bottom, the head held by a metal rim, commonly about thirty-three and thirty-five centimetres across. The player, called a timbalero, usually stands at the stand and strikes the heads and the shells with wooden sticks, occasionally using the hands. The instrument is common in dance music and bands such as danzón, mambo and chachachá, keeping the beat with the shell pattern or with a cowbell or cymbal, and using rolls, rim shots and similar devices in fills and solos.
蒂姆巴雷斯鼓源自十九世紀傳入古巴的定音鼓，先用於典型管樂團；後以金屬鍋、豬油罐製: The timbales come from the timpani that reached Cuba in the nineteenth century, first used in the orquestas típicas; later shallower single-headed drums were made from metal pots and lard tins and played with straight sticks. In the mid-1920s, when Havana banned the bongo, small timbalitos appeared in its place; after the charanga replaced the orquesta típica, the timbales became its core. In the 1930s Ulpiano Díaz added the cowbell and promoted the fan-shaped stroke; in the 1950s the instrument developed in Havana nightclubs and jam sessions under the influence of the jazz drum kit. In the 1970s songo bands brought in rumba and funk and mixed the timbales with the drum kit; in the 1990s teaching videos appeared. After that, Ubaldo Nieto, Tito Puente and others spread it through New York, Latin jazz, mambo, salsa, Latin rock, reggae and hip hop.

The heads were calfskin early on and are now mostly plastic, for greater volume and durability, and are fixed on steel rims. The playing sticks are wooden. The sources do not state the materials of the stand, the cowbell and the other parts, so no guess is made.
蒂姆巴雷斯鼓為淺身單面膜鳴鼓，金屬鼓殼；相較單面嗵鼓，鼓身較淺，通常調音較高，尤: The timbales are shallow single-headed membranophones with metal shells; against the single-headed tom they are shallower and usually tuned higher, especially for their size. On range, the source notes only that the tuning is higher, and that the two drums differ in average diameter. The player strikes head and shell with wooden sticks and uses rim shots and rolls, which gives a wide percussion range; the shell note, the cowbell and the cymbal usually carry the rhythm. Plastic heads raise the volume and the durability, and the drums are sometimes struck by hand. Unlike the classical timpani, it is not played with soft-headed mallets but struck with straight sticks, which is why shell notes and rim shots are possible.
